sentences.text: Eotyrannus is a genus of tyrannosauroid theropod dinosaur, a name that translates to "dawn tyrant".
This predator possessed unique skeletal features, including a concave notch on the lower jaw bone and a tear-drop shaped cross-section on its forearm bones.
It holds the record for the proportionally longest hands known in any theropod dinosaur to date.
Unlike advanced tyrannosaurids, this animal retained primitive traits such as elongated neck vertebrae, long well-developed arms, and an unornamented dorsal skull surface.
The exact location where the holotype was found remains unrevealed to protect the site from erosion and allow for future collection.
Its scientific name references its famous relative, Tyrannosaurus rex, and means "first tyrant".
The fossil was found in a plant debris clay bed after local collector Gavin Leng discovered a claw in 1995 and brought it to Steve Hutt.
The specific epithet of Eotyrannus honors Gavin Leng, the collector who discovered the initial claw.
Eotyrannus was discovered in 1996 by amateur fossil collector Gavin Leng on the southwest coast of the Isle of Wight in the Wessex Formation of the Wealden Group in the United Kingdom.
The discovery was initially just loose teeth, and it was not confirmed as a new genus until a jaw fragment was found.
Approximately 40% of the total skeleton has been found, which is sufficient to determine it belongs entirely to a new species.
A detailed monograph describing the specimen was published in the journal PeerJ in 2022.
The holotype specimen measures up to 4.5 meters in length, though it represents a subadult rather than an adult.
The nasal bones of Eotyrannus were fused together.
The holotype specimen disarticulated before fossilization, with no part of the vertebral column preserved in articulation, indicating the individual was immature.
Eotyrannus likely fed on contemporary mammals such as Yaverlestes and Eobaatar.
This predator likely hunted ornithopods such as Hypsilophodon and Iguanodon.
Before a specific fragment was correctly identified as the distal tibia, Eotyrannus was reconstructed with much longer tibiae, influencing early reconstructions of the animal.
In 2024, Andrea Cau recovered Eotyrannus as a sister taxon to Proceratosauridae, distant from Megaraptora.
Eotyrannus is classified within the family Stokesosauridae.
A recent 2014 analysis by Porfiri et al. found that Eotyrannus is a megaraptorian closely related to taxa like Megaraptor.
Eotyrannus lived in the Early Cretaceous Wessex Formation on the southwest coast of the Isle of Wight, United Kingdom.
Eotyrannus lived in Europe during the Early Cretaceous, approximately 125 to 120 million years ago in the Barremian stage.
The paleoclimate had a mean annual temperature of 20–25 °C with low seasonal rainfall.
Eotyrannus lived during the Hauterivian to Barremian stages, from 132.6 to 121.4 million years ago.
The discovery of Eotyrannus in Europe questions the purported Asian origin of tyrannosauroids and argues for a more complex biogeography.
The discovery of this animal in Europe raises interesting questions about the supposed Asian origin of these animals.
It is debated whether the large size of the animal signifies early evolution of the trait for this clade or if Eotyrannus developed the trait independently.
